"Dint" is a word with two related meanings. One is older and refers to a physical mark; the other is the more famous one that you'll actually encounter in real life — and it lives almost entirely inside a single, fixed phrase: "by dint of."
Meaning 1: A Dent or Mark from a Blow

In its most literal, physical sense, a dint is a hollow or depression made on a surface when something strikes or presses against it hard. Think of the shallow crater left on metal when you hit it with a hammer, or the crushed-in spot on a car door after a collision. That mark — that indentation — is a dint.

This is actually the same word as "dent," and in older English they were used interchangeably. Today, "dent" has completely taken over for this physical meaning, and "dint" in this sense sounds archaic. You might encounter it in older literature, but you'd almost never use it this way in everyday speech or writing today.

Example:

"The knight's shield bore the dints of a hundred battles."

(= the dents and marks left by blows in battle)
Meaning 2: Force, Power, or Means — "By Dint of"

This is the meaning that is very much alive today, and it's the one worth learning thoroughly.

From the idea of a blow landing with force, the word dint came to mean force or power itself. Over time, this gave birth to the phrase "by dint of," which means:

"by means of" / "through the power or effort of" / "because of"

When you say someone achieved something by dint of something, you're saying that thing was the driving force — the means — that made the achievement happen. There is often a subtle flavor of effort, persistence, or hard-won struggle in the phrase, though not always.

Think of it this way:
"By dint of X" = "X was the force that made it happen. X is how it got done."
Examples of "By Dint of" in Use

"She passed the exam by dint of sheer determination."

(= Her determination was the force that got her through. She passed through determination alone.)

"He built his fortune by dint of years of relentless work."

(= Years of relentless work were what produced his fortune.)

"The small country gained international respect by dint of its excellent healthcare system."

(= It earned that respect through its excellent healthcare system.)

"By dint of careful saving over decades, they finally bought a home."

(= Careful saving over decades was what made buying a home possible.)
The Tone and Register of "By Dint of"

This phrase is formal and literary. You would not say it in casual conversation — it would sound stiff and out of place. Instead, you'll find it in:

  • Formal essays and academic writing
  • Literary fiction and historical writing
  • Journalism and opinion pieces that want to sound elevated
  • Speeches or oratory

In casual speech, people simply say "because of," "through," "thanks to," or "by means of." The phrase "by dint of" adds weight and a slight old-fashioned dignity to the sentence. Writers reach for it when they want to stress that something was achieved through real force, effort, or a specific mechanism.
What Makes "By Dint of" Different from "By Means of"?

They are very close in meaning, and often interchangeable. But there are subtle differences:

  • "By means of" is neutral. It simply describes the method or tool used. ("He opened the lock by means of a key.")
  • "By dint of" carries a slightly stronger sense of effort, persistence, or force being applied. It often implies the thing wasn't easy — that it took sustained power to make it happen. ("She carved out a career by dint of decades of sacrifice.")

You wouldn't naturally say "by dint of a key" — because using a key takes no special effort. But you would say "by dint of sheer willpower" — because willpower being the deciding force fits the word's flavor perfectly.

One Line to Remember It By

"By dint of" = "by the force of" — and from there, "by means of."

If you ever see this phrase in a book or article, just substitute "through" or "by means of" in your mind, and the sentence will make perfect sense.
